scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Theeyaattam developed as an hereditary temple art in Kerala, practiced exclusively by specialized temple-bound communities.
Bhadrakali Theeyaattu belongs to the Theeyaattunni community in south-central Kerala, centered around temples such as Pallippurathu Kavu in Kottayam and Thrikkariyoor Mahadeva Temple.
Ayyappan Theeyaattu is maintained by Thiyyadi Nambiars in central Kerala, whose ancestral lineage experts trace to 18th-century migrations from north Malabar.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Bhadrakali Theeyaattu depicts the mythological victory of Goddess Bhadrakali over the demon Darikasura.
Ayyappan Theeyaattu enacts the birth story of Lord Ayyappa, born of Shiva and Vishnu in Mohini form.
The performance functions as an annual festival highlight or family offering, culminating in the distribution of kalam powder as divine prasadam and trance revelations called kalpana.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance begins with minimal footwork during the dramatic Koothu phase, relying on hand gestures that resemble less refined forms of Koodiyattam and Kathakali with neutral facial expressions.
During the Velichchappaadu phase, the oracle holds a small sword and initiates slow, measured steps while circumambulating the floor painting.
Over 9 or 11 counter-clockwise circles, the movement tempo steadily accelerates until the oracle leaps onto the sacred powder image in a frenzy.
Watch for Kalam Circumambulation, Kalam Erasing.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music accompanies every phase following the floor painting.
Songs blend old Malayalam and Tamil texts set to endemic Kerala tunes, classical Sopanam ragas, and Carnatic melodic structures.
Listen for the chenda, para, ilathalam.
The pulse is Flexible metric cycles changing from slow devotional invocations to rapid drum pulses at about 110 beats a minute.
Resonant, deep drum beats from para and chenda interspersed with the bright metallic clatter of ilathalam cymbals, accompanied by archaic vocal chants in Sopanam ragas.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Performances occur on consecrated temple floors in front of a lighted nilavilakku brass lamp.
In Bhadrakali performance, the male dancer adopts goddess attire and turns away from the lamp.
In Ayyappan Koothu, dancers wear defined attire without facial paint.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Mulankunnathukavu Thiyyaadi Raman Nambiar is a prominent author and practitioner who documented the tradition in his book 'Ayyappan Theeyattu', written with support from V. R. Prabodhachandran Nayar.
Bhadrakali Theeyaattu is concentrated in south-central Kerala (Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, and Ernakulam districts).
Bhadrakali Theeyaattu is inherited and transmitted through male members of the Theeyaattunni Brahmin community.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Theeyaattam is a sacred temple ritual governed by strict traditional codes. Outsiders must not disrupt the sacred floor painting (kalam), touch ritual items, or attempt to imitate the trance rituals outside proper temple contexts.

scenes.title: Until next time
narration: In the sacred temples of Kerala, hereditary artists spent hours painting a deity in colored powders, only to dance it into dust before midnight.
